INTERVIEW STATEMENT - CHAD MCKENZIE

I have not been comfortable with the growing assumption that every classroom activity should include artificial intelligence. New technology can be useful, but I think we are moving too quickly and overlooking serious problems. Students sometimes treat an AI response as if it were an authoritative source, even when the output contains errors, invented details, or advice that does not fit the situation. That makes me nervous, particularly in courses where accuracy and careful procedure matter.

I also dislike how easily these systems can blur the line between assistance and substitution. A student may begin by asking for a hint and end up submitting an entire generated response. When that happens, the assignment no longer tells me what the student can actually do. It is disappointing for instructors who have spent time building meaningful exercises, and it is unfair to classmates who complete the work themselves.

Another problem is that AI can make weak work look stronger than it is. Professional wording and clean formatting can create the impression of understanding without the underlying knowledge. Then, when the student has to explain the answer in person or perform the task without assistance, the gap becomes obvious. I would rather see an imperfect answer that honestly shows a student's thinking because that gives us something real to teach from.

I realize AI will continue to exist in the workplace, so I am not arguing that students should never learn about it. My concern is with uncontrolled use before foundational skills are established. I want stricter limits, more independent demonstrations, and clearer accountability. At this point, the problems I have seen make me cautious and often frustrated rather than optimistic. If we cannot be confident that AI is supporting learning instead of bypassing it, I would prefer to restrict it rather than encourage it.
